notes:
I've organised these notes verse by verse, with the URL after each point. Some gaps to know about first:

- **Missing sources:** I couldn't read Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org), OCA/Orthodox sources, catholic.com, the Haydock Catholic commentary, Wesley's own Notes, or the bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org scholarly notes.
- **Popular teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Enduring Word cut off:** the full Enduring Word page stopped at v. 17, so for vv. 18–23 I've used only the parts shown in search results.
- **Labels are mine:** where I name a commentator's tradition (e.g. Clarke as Methodist), that's my own identification. The pages don't say it.

---

**v. 1–3**
- After the golden calf, God still let Israel go on to the Promised Land. If they challenged God – pleading with Him for His presence, not only His blessings – it would show a genuine heart for God Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- **Who is the angel (v. 2)? The commentators disagree.** Guzik says the angel in Exodus 33:2 was just an angelic being, not the LORD himself. Guzik also quotes Cole, who reads the later promise (v. 14) as meaning the messenger becomes "the angel of his presence," a full showing of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- **Stiff-necked:** God would have brought them under the yoke of his law, and into the bond of his covenant, but their necks were too stiff to bow to them. (Matthew Henry) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm

**v. 4–6**
- The people grieved at losing God's close presence, not just his gifts. Guzik quotes Morgan: "It is clear that the people felt that the promise of an angel to be sent before them was the lowering of a privilege." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- Taking off their jewellery showed repentance. It was not a time to decorate the outside but to set the heart right. Guzik adds, quoting Cole, that the same ornaments later went to build the tabernacle (Exodus 35:22). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- Henry says that of all sin's results, true penitents most lament, and dread most, is God's departure from them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm

**v. 7**
- Keil and Delitzsch say this tent was not the tabernacle of Exodus 25 (not yet built). It was Moses' own tent, made a temporary sanctuary because the cloud came down on it. They give two reasons Moses pitched it outside the camp: to deepen the people's repentance by showing their separation from God, and to keep a way open to the LORD so the covenant could be renewed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm
- Cole (quoted by Guzik) notes that ancient sanctuaries usually stood outside towns, so Israel had lost its uniqueness as the nation with God in its very midst. Guzik adds that anyone seeking God now had to separate themselves at a cost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/

**v. 8–10**
- The people watched Moses go to worship, and then worshipped too. Guzik compares the cloud to a royal flag showing that the king is present. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the cloud came down when Moses went in as mediator, a sign that his advocacy prevailed, that Israel's sin was forgiven, and that God would again be gracious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): The cloudy pillar which had withdrawn from the camp when it was polluted with idolatry, now returned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm

**v. 11**
- **"Face to face":** Benson and Poole say God has no literal face. It means God spoke freely and directly with Moses, not through dreams, visions or an angel as with other prophets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: God was present, but not under any visible form. https://biblehub.com/exodus/33-11.htm
- Gill reads it more strongly, as a real visible appearance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-11.html
- Clarke says there was no bodily appearance, only familiar speech in words Moses could understand. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-11.html
- Calvin (quoted by Keil and Delitzsch) says God showed himself in a special form but never in his own full glory, only as much as human weakness could bear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm
- Ellicott: the privilege was unique to Moses, but in what exactly the peculiarity consisted is not apparent. https://biblehub.com/exodus/33-11.htm
- **Was it the pre-incarnate Christ?** GotQuestions sees two options, a Christophany or a figure of speech, and prefers the figure of speech. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-Moses-face-to-face.html Guzik says God appearing in human form is possible but a figurative meaning is more likely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- **Joshua:** Pulpit thinks he was given the tent because he alone had no part in the calf. Benson and Poole say Aaron and the elders were temporarily set aside for the idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm
- Gill mentions another reading in which Joshua went back to camp with Moses and it was the LORD who "departed not" from the tent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-11.htm

**v. 12–13**
- Moses was bold, almost rude, but he based his boldness on grace God had already shown him. Guzik also notes how often the word "know" comes up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- Henry: Moses pleads that the people are still God's own, as "My child is foolish and froward, but he is my child, and I cannot abandon him." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm
- Bible.org treats "let me know Your ways" (v. 13) and "show me Your glory" (v. 18) as essentially the same request. https://bible.org/seriespage/29-backside-god-exodus-3318-349

**v. 14**
- "My Presence" is literally "My Face." The rest God promises means peace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/

**v. 15–16**
- Henry paraphrases Moses: "Better lie down and die here in the wilderness than go forward to Canaan without God's presence." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm
- Only God's presence, not any gift, would make Israel different from the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/

**v. 17**
- Calvin: God adds nothing new, but confirms by repetition what He had just said, in order to remove all doubt. https://www.ccel.org/study/Exodus_33:17-23
- Henry: Moses wanted a promise for the people, not just for himself, and he got it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm

**v. 18**
- Henry says Moses knew God's essence can't be seen with physical eyes, and wanted some visible sign of the glory. Henry also suggests that perhaps there was in it a mixture of human infirmity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm
- Guzik reports Spurgeon comparing Moses to Peter at the Transfiguration, asking without fully understanding. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/
- Keil and Delitzsch: Moses wanted more than any earlier showing of God's glory, even more than the "face to face" talks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm

**v. 19**
- **Goodness as glory:** Guzik says God's glory lies in His goodness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-33/ Henry (Concise) says God wants to be known by the glory of his mercy more than by his majesty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm Bible.org explains "goodness" as God's kindness and generosity. https://bible.org/seriespage/29-backside-god-exodus-3318-349
- **"Mercy on whom I have mercy," which Paul quotes in Romans 9:15. The emphasis differs:**
  - Henry: these words, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, do as fully express the absolute prerogative and sovereignty of his will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/9-15.html
  - Barnes: God gives mercy as a sovereign and owes no one an account of his choice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/9-15.html
  - Clarke (a Methodist) ties it to God sparing the Jewish nation after the idolatry, when they deserved to be cut off. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/romans/9-15.html
  - People's New Testament: as Paul uses it, the verse says God favors nations according to his pleasure. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/romans/9-18.html
  - Keil and Delitzsch: Paul uses it to overturn the claims of self-righteous Jews to share in the Messiah's salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
  - I couldn't find the Reformed and Wesleyan teachers on their own sites (e.g. Ligonier or Seedbed) arguing this verse directly.

**v. 20**
- Henry: seeing God fully would overwhelm any mortal. Man is weak and could not bear it, guilty and could not but dread it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_033.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch: God is a consuming fire to unholy people, and our earthly bodies set a limit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- Coffman: no exception was ever made, not even for Moses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-20.html
- Precept Austin links this verse to John 1:18. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-33-commentary

**v. 21–22**
- **Rock and cleft as pictures of Christ:** Henry says this was the rock at Horeb, and Paul says "that rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-22.html Henry (Concise) adds that the cleft may stand for Christ smitten and crucified. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- The scene inspired Toplady's hymn "Rock of Ages." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/exodus/exodus-33.cfm
- Calvin likens the cleft to a narrow window: we are shut in our bodies, so God lights us indirectly and we see him only from behind. https://www.ccel.org/study/Exodus_33:17-23
- Keil and Delitzsch place the scene on the summit of Sinai (Exodus 34:2). Some link the cleft to Elijah's cave (1 Kings 19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm

**v. 23**
- **"My back" means a partial view.** Poole: Moses saw God imperfectly, the way you see only a person's back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: the back means the reflection of glory that had just passed by. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- Pulpit: the body language is a "strong" accommodation to human ideas. It rejects Kalisch's view that the back means God's works as fanciful, and not borne out by the context. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- Others accept the "works" view. A Calvin-attributed note on StudyLight calls the back parts the shadow God casts as he passes by in his works. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-21.html
- Gill lists several readings: Christ's humanity, God's works in creation, or (his preference) our partial knowledge of God in this life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/33-23.htm
- Henry: Moses later saw Christ's face shining at the Transfiguration. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/33-22.html
- Bible.org: the back is God's goodness and his "face" may be his severity. It also quotes Gispen that this may have been a prophecy of the incarnation. https://bible.org/seriespage/29-backside-god-exodus-3318-349
- Hard Sayings (quoted on Precept Austin) says it may mean the afterglow, or the outline of a figure walking away. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-33-commentary
- **Church Fathers (Orthodox/Catholic heritage):** Gregory Nazianzen says he saw God's back parts while sheltered by the Rock, the Word that was made flesh for us. He calls them tokens God leaves behind, like the sun reflected in water. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310228.htm
